countries.country_overview: Australia operates one of the most liberalised foreign-exchange regimes in the world. There are no general exchange controls or restrictions on current or capital account transactions for residents or non-residents. The framework is administered by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) and the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC).

summary.traveler: Travelers may bring in or take out unlimited amounts of Australian Dollars and foreign currency. No general currency declaration is required for normal travel amounts.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals enjoy full freedom to hold, transfer, convert and repatriate foreign currency through authorised banks and financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Unlimited amounts of Australian Dollars and foreign currency may be brought into Australia with no general declaration requirement for travelers.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Unlimited amounts of Australian Dollars and foreign currency may be taken out of Australia. Residents must comply with RBA limits when exporting large sums of foreign currency.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: No mandatory currency declaration threshold applies for ordinary travelers. Movements of AUD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) in cash or bearer negotiable instruments must be reported to AUSTRAC under anti-money laundering rules.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Australian residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in foreign currency or AUD. Cross-border payments and repatriation of funds are handled freely through authorised financial institutions.
rules.exchange_controls: Australia maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised for both current and capital account transactions.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks, licensed money exchange houses, and ATMs throughout Australia.

countries.country_overview: Canada operates a fully liberalised foreign-exchange regime under the regulatory authority of the Bank of Canada and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC). There are no general exchange controls or restrictions on current or capital account transactions for residents or non-residents. The Canadian Dollar is freely convertible.

summary.traveler: Travelers may bring in or take out unlimited amounts of Canadian Dollars and foreign currency. Cash movements of CAD 10,000 or more must be reported to the Canada Border Services Agency.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals enjoy full freedom to hold, transfer, convert and repatriate foreign currency through authorised banks and financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency may be freely imported into Canada without restriction. Reporting of CAD 10,000 or more is mandatory and should be made using form E677 to CBSA before clearance, either at airport pre-security (for air) or at the border checkpoint (land/rail/boat).
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Residents and non-residents may freely export foreign currency previously declared or documented. Canadian residents exporting CAD 10,000 or more must report to CBSA (form E677). Non-residents need only verify the amount was lawfully imported. No repatriation restrictions apply.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: CAD 10,000 or more (or equivalent in foreign currency or bearer negotiable instruments) at entry and exit. Reporting is mandatory to the Canada Border Services Agency.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Canadian residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in Canadian Dollars or foreign currency through authorised financial institutions.
rules.exchange_controls: Canada maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised for both current and capital account transactions.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks and authorised dealers throughout Canada.

rules.resident_holding_rules: French residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.

rules.exchange_controls: France maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised within the Eurozone framework.

countries.country_overview: India operates a statutory foreign-exchange framework under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, administered principally by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). In practice this is not a discretionary retail-cash jurisdiction: lawful foreign-exchange activity typically routes through authorised dealer banks while border cash controls are exercised through CBIC Indian Customs declarations (including the Currency Declaration Form, CDF) when thresholds apply. Relative to freely convertible regimes, India's FX regime mixes liberalisation on much of the current account with materially tighter regulation on the capital account; users should assume documentation, channels, and transaction-specific approvals matter.

summary.traveler: Any person may bring foreign exchange into India without limit. Declaration on the Currency Declaration Form (CDF) is required if foreign currency notes exceed USD 5,000 or the aggregate foreign exchange exceeds USD 10,000.
summary.business: All cross-border trade and capital transactions must be routed through Authorised Dealer banks under FEMA. The 2026 regulations introduce targeted updates for exports, imports, service payments and related operations.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: There is ordinarily no prohibition on importing foreign exchange into India, but lawful physical import is framed around declaration and documentation: when foreign currency notes exceed USD 5,000 or aggregate foreign exchange (including traveller instruments in scope of the Currency Declaration Form) exceeds USD 10,000 on arrival, the Currency Declaration Form (CDF) pathway becomes operationally decisive. Practical compliance means carrying supporting documentation consistent with Customs guidance and preserving CDF linkage if you intend to reconvert or carry unutilised foreign exchange outward later.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Unspent foreign exchange declared on arrival may be taken out, and the Currency Declaration Form should be retained for reconversion or for taking unused foreign exchange out of India.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The operative arrival-side threshold framing in the Customs materials bundled with Currency Declaration Form (CDF) practice is USD 5,000 for foreign currency notes and USD 10,000 for aggregate foreign exchange (including notes/travellers’ cheques falling under the form’s stated scope). When either threshold applies, Customs expects the relevant declaration channel/process to be followed; travellers should preserve endorsed documentation because it anchors later authorised-dealer conversions and outbound movements.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Indian residents remain subject to FEMA-based limits and conditions in relation to holding and using foreign exchange. Users should verify account eligibility, retention limits, and transaction-specific permissions directly with RBI rules and the authorised dealer.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents (including NRIs and PIOs) may maintain NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO accounts with repatriation rights as permitted under RBI guidelines.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Import, export, and related cross-border service transactions must be handled through Authorised Dealer banks in accordance with FEMA regulations and the applicable RBI framework.
rules.exchange_controls: India maintains a regulated exchange framework under FEMA 1999. Current account transactions are largely liberalised while capital account transactions are subject to regulation and reporting.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange transactions are executed through Authorised Dealer banks, licensed money changers and authorised airports. The Currency Declaration Form (CDF) must be retained for reconversion and compliance purposes.

countries.country_overview: Italy is a euro-area member of the European Union. Cross-border movements of cash are administered by the Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM), the Italian customs authority, together with the Guardia di Finanza, under Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 for cash entering or leaving the European Union and under Legislative Decree 195/2008 (Article 3) for cash entering or leaving Italian national territory, including movements to and from other EU Member States. The euro is legal tender and Italy applies no national exchange-control approval regime; within the EU legal framework the free movement of capital is guaranteed under Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, subject to Treaty exceptions and to sanctions, anti-money-laundering, tax, reporting and prudential controls rather than exchange controls. Banking, payment and conversion services are provided by intermediaries authorised and supervised by Banca d'Italia within the Eurosystem.

summary.traveler: Travellers carrying cash of EUR 10,000 or more must lodge a declaration with the Italian customs authority (ADM) at the first border customs office. The obligation applies both to cash entering or leaving the European Union (Article 3, Regulation (EU) 2018/1672) and to cash entering or leaving Italian national territory, including movements to or from other EU Member States (Article 3, Legislative Decree 195/2008). 'Cash' covers currency (banknotes and coins), bearer-negotiable instruments, and goods used as highly liquid stores of value such as gold.
summary.business: Italy applies no national exchange-control regime: under Article 63 TFEU restrictions on capital movements and payments are prohibited, subject to Treaty exceptions (taxation, prudential supervision, declaration procedures, certain third-country measures and safeguards) and to sanctions, anti-money-laundering, tax and reporting rules. Cross-border payments, foreign-currency accounts and conversion are routed through banks, payment institutions and electronic-money institutions authorised and supervised by Banca d'Italia, without any guarantee of a specific account or service. The EUR 10,000 cross-border cash-declaration regimes are separate from this capital-movement framework.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Cash of EUR 10,000 or more brought into Italy must be declared to the Italian customs authority (ADM) at the first border customs office. Where the traveller enters the European Union through Italy the obligation arises under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672; where the traveller enters Italian national territory from another EU Member State it arises under Article 3 of Legislative Decree 195/2008. 'Cash' includes currency, bearer-negotiable instruments and gold used as a highly liquid store of value.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Cash of EUR 10,000 or more taken out of Italy must be declared to the Italian customs authority (ADM) at the first border customs office. The obligation applies on leaving the European Union through Italy (Article 3, Regulation (EU) 2018/1672) and on leaving Italian national territory towards another EU Member State (Article 3, Legislative Decree 195/2008). The same cash categories apply; a declaration with inexact or incomplete information does not satisfy the obligation.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The threshold for a mandatory declaration of accompanied cash carried by a traveller is EUR 10,000 or more. Two parallel regimes apply and are administered through a single ADM declaration form: Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 for cash entering or leaving the European Union, and Article 3 of Legislative Decree 195/2008 for cash entering or leaving Italian national territory (including to and from other EU Member States). Unaccompanied cash sent by post, freight or courier is covered separately by Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 (disclosure on the request of customs). Customs may require production of the cash and apply administrative seizure; specific penalty amounts are fixed by Legislative Decree 195/2008.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Within the EU Treaty framework, general restrictions on capital movements and payments are prohibited (Article 63 TFEU), and no Italy-specific general prior-approval exchange-control regime applies to residents holding or transferring foreign currency. This does not guarantee that any given resident may open any particular foreign-currency account: holding and transferring funds remain subject to sanctions, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, taxation, reporting, prudential rules (Article 65 TFEU), and each supervised intermediary's own conditions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Article 63 TFEU prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments both between Member States and with third countries, so no general exchange-control restriction applies to non-residents holding accounts or transferring funds in Italy. This creates no entitlement to an account or service: onboarding, taxation, sanctions screening, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, reporting, and each institution's conditions apply, and the Treaty preserves certain third-country exceptions (Articles 64 and 65 TFEU).
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Cross-border business payments and settlement are not subject to a general exchange-control approval regime; under Article 63 TFEU payments between Member States and with third countries are free of restriction, subject to the Treaty's exceptions and to sanctions, anti-money-laundering, tax and reporting rules. Such payments are routed through banks, payment institutions and electronic-money institutions authorised and supervised by Banca d'Italia. This framework does not by itself establish an unrestricted choice of invoice currency, which depends on the contract and applicable rules.
rules.exchange_controls: Italy maintains no national exchange-control regime for capital movements or payments. Under Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, all restrictions on the movement of capital and on payments, between Member States and with third countries, are prohibited. This is not unconditional: the Treaty preserves exceptions, including measures on taxation and the prudential supervision of financial services and declaration procedures for administrative or statistical purposes (Article 65), the option to maintain certain restrictions on direct investment involving third countries (Article 64), and temporary safeguard measures (Article 66), alongside EU restrictive measures (sanctions). This capital-movement framework is separate from the EUR 10,000 cross-border cash-declaration regimes.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Currency conversion and cross-border payment services in Italy are provided through banks, payment institutions and electronic-money institutions authorised and supervised by Banca d'Italia, which maintains the supervisory registers of these intermediaries. Authorisation and supervision establish the regulatory routing; they do not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price. Access remains subject to each intermediary's onboarding, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, sanctions screening, and reporting requirements.

countries.country_overview: Japan operates a fully liberalised foreign-exchange regime under the regulatory authority of the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and the Bank of Japan (BOJ). The Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act (FEFTA) governs the framework. There are no general exchange controls for current or capital account transactions for residents or non-residents. The yen is freely convertible and Japan maintains one of the most open FX regimes among major economies.

summary.traveler: Travelers may bring in or take out unlimited amounts of Japanese Yen and foreign currency. No general currency declaration is required for normal travel amounts.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals enjoy full freedom to hold, transfer, convert and repatriate foreign currency through authorised banks and financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Unlimited amounts of Japanese Yen and foreign currency may be brought into Japan. No general declaration is required for travelers under normal circumstances.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: When departing Japan, travelers may export unlimited amounts of Japanese Yen and foreign currency. Large cash amounts may require reporting under anti-money laundering rules.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: No mandatory declaration threshold applies for ordinary travelers. Movements of JPY 1,000,000 or more (or equivalent) may trigger reporting requirements under AML regulations.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Japanese residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in Japanese Yen or foreign currency. Cross-border payments and repatriation of funds are handled freely through authorised financial institutions.
rules.exchange_controls: Japan maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised for both current and capital account transactions.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks, licensed money exchange houses, and ATMs throughout Japan.

summary.traveler: Travelers may bring in foreign currency without limit. Cash movements of USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared to Pakistan Customs.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals may hold, transfer and repatriate foreign currency through authorised dealers in accordance with SBP rules.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Travelers entering Pakistan may import any amount of foreign currency without restriction. Cash or monetary instruments of USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared to Pakistan Customs upon arrival.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Travelers departing Pakistan may export foreign currency up to the amount they declared on arrival or obtained through authorised channels. Export of Pakistani Rupees is generally restricted.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent in foreign currency or bearer negotiable instruments) at entry and exit. Declaration is mandatory to Pakistan Customs.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Pakistani residents may maintain foreign currency accounts with authorised banks subject to SBP regulations.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely through authorised dealers.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in foreign currency through authorised dealers in accordance with SBP guidelines.
rules.exchange_controls: Pakistan maintains no general exchange controls on current account transactions. Capital account transactions are regulated by the State Bank of Pakistan.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are available through authorised banks and exchange companies across Pakistan.

countries.country_overview: South Africa operates a floating exchange-rate regime administered by the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) through its Financial Surveillance Department. Cross-border foreign-exchange transactions are conducted through Authorised Dealers under the Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers. Current-account transactions are largely liberalised, while certain capital-account movements remain subject to exchange controls, prior approval or reporting requirements. Traveller currency movements are enforced at the border by SARS Customs under the Exchange Control Regulations, 1961.

summary.traveler: Travellers may bring foreign currency into South Africa without limit, subject to declaration. South African bank notes may be taken out up to R25,000, and are unlimited only when travelling within the Common Monetary Area; carrying rand above R25,000 requires prior SARB authorisation. Any currency — rand or foreign currency convertible to rand — in excess of R100,000 is treated as excess currency requiring written SARB permission before entering or leaving. The traveller declaration is administered by SARS through an online form or the manual Traveller Declaration (TD-01).
summary.business: Businesses must route cross-border foreign-exchange transactions through Authorised Dealers (banks) appointed by the SARB, in accordance with the Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers. Current-account payments are largely liberalised, while certain capital-account transfers, repatriation and offshore investment remain subject to SARB exchange-control approval, documentation and reporting.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency may be brought into South Africa without limit. Travellers must declare the currency in their possession; the traveller declaration is administered by SARS through an online declaration form or the manual Traveller Declaration (TD-01). Any amount in excess of R100,000 — rand or foreign currency convertible to rand — is treated as excess currency under the Exchange Control Regulations and requires prior written permission from the SARB.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: South African bank notes may be taken out up to R25,000, and are unlimited only when travelling within the Common Monetary Area; carrying rand above R25,000 requires prior authorisation from the SARB. Currency in excess of R100,000, whether rand or foreign currency convertible to rand, requires written SARB permission. A traveller leaving South Africa must declare the currency in their possession to SARS Customs, which may search and seize currency under the Exchange Control Regulations.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: Two distinct thresholds apply and must not be conflated. First, the SARB rand-carrying limit: South African bank notes above R25,000 may not be taken out without prior SARB authorisation, and are unlimited only within the Common Monetary Area. Second, the SARB excess-currency rule: any amount, rand or foreign currency convertible to rand, in excess of R100,000 requires written SARB permission before entering or leaving. Separately, the traveller declaration — covering bank notes, foreign currency, securities and gold — is administered by SARS via an online form or the manual TD-01.
rules.resident_holding_rules: South African residents transact foreign exchange through Authorised Dealers under the Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers. Resident individuals are accorded a single discretionary allowance of R2 million per calendar year and a foreign capital allowance of R10 million per applicant per calendar year; the foreign capital allowance and larger transfers are subject to the South African Revenue Service Tax Compliance Status (TCS) process. These two annual allowance limits may not be exceeded.
rules.non_resident_rules: Exchange controls on non-residents have been abolished, and qualifying non-resident income and securities proceeds are freely transferable. Non-residents transact through Non-resident Rand accounts and vostro accounts held by Authorised Dealers, and funds introduced from abroad may be retransferred. Certain transactions still require documentary evidence and settlement through approved channels.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Cross-border business settlement is effected through Authorised Dealers appointed by the SARB, in accordance with the Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers. Current-account payments are largely liberalised, while capital-account transfers, cross-border loans and offshore investment remain subject to SARB exchange-control approval, documentation and reporting.
rules.exchange_controls: South Africa maintains a floating exchange-rate regime with exchange controls administered by the SARB Financial Surveillance Department under the Exchange Control Regulations, 1961. Current-account transactions are largely liberalised; certain capital-account movements remain subject to controls, prior approval and reporting.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign-exchange conversion and cross-border transfers are handled by Authorised Dealers appointed by the SARB. Authorised Dealers perform customer due diligence under section 21 of the Financial Intelligence Centre Act, and all cross-border transactions are reported through the SARB Reporting System using the prescribed purpose codes.

countries.country_overview: South Korea operates a floating exchange-rate regime for the Korean won, with the Bank of Korea (BOK) as the central bank and the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MOEF) responsible for the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act (FETA). Cross-border movements of cash by travellers are administered by the Korea Customs Service, which requires a mandatory declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000. Under FETA, current-account payments and receipts are substantially liberalised, while capital transactions involving large fund movements are subject to transaction-specific notification or permission procedures handled through foreign exchange banks, the Bank of Korea Governor, or MOEF. The Korean won is not fully internationalised. This is a regulated framework, not an absence of exchange controls.

summary.traveler: Travellers entering or leaving South Korea must file a mandatory declaration with the Korea Customs Service when their means of payment — foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks combined — exceed USD 10,000 in total; the traveller marks item no. 3 of the Traveler Declaration Form and receives a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration. At or below USD 10,000 no declaration is required. This customs declaration is separate from the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act reporting that applies to capital transfers.
summary.business: Under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, current-account payments and receipts are substantially liberalised, while capital transactions (FETA Article 18) and certain methods of payment or receipt (FETA Article 16) require transaction-specific reporting, and some payments to foreign countries may require permission (FETA Article 15). The Minister of Economy and Finance (MOEF) is the competent authority under the Act; FETA Article 23 delegates specified powers to the Financial Services Commission, the Bank of Korea Governor, the Financial Supervisory Service Governor and foreign exchange agencies, and the actual filing or permission destination — a foreign exchange bank, the Bank of Korea Governor, or MOEF — depends on the transaction type and the applicable Act, Enforcement Decree and Regulations. Cross-border payments and foreign-currency accounts run through foreign exchange businesses registered under FETA Article 8. These FETA regimes are separate from the Korea Customs USD 10,000 border declaration, foreign exchange banks' reporting of foreign-currency sales over USD 10,000 to the National Tax Service (FETA Article 21), and KoFIU anti-money-laundering reporting.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: A traveller bringing means of payment into South Korea — foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks combined — exceeding USD 10,000 in total must file a mandatory declaration with the Korea Customs Service, marking item no. 3 of the Traveler Declaration Form and receiving a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration. At or below USD 10,000 no permission or declaration is required. This customs declaration is distinct from any Foreign Exchange Transactions Act reporting on capital transactions.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: A traveller leaving South Korea must likewise file a mandatory Korea Customs declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000 in total. Separately, under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, capital-account transfers by residents may require transaction-specific notification or permission through a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor; that reporting is distinct from the customs border declaration.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The Korea Customs declaration threshold is means of payment exceeding USD 10,000 in total — aggregating foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks — for a traveller entering or leaving the country; it is a mandatory report to Customs (Traveler Declaration Form item no. 3, yielding a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration), not merely a document to produce if questioned, and it is triggered only above USD 10,000. This border declaration is separate from three other regimes: Foreign Exchange Transactions Act capital-transaction notification or permission, foreign exchange banks' reporting of FX sales over USD 10,000 to the National Tax Service, and KoFIU anti-money-laundering reporting.
rules.resident_holding_rules: South Korean residents may open and hold foreign-currency accounts — resident accounts and resident foreign currency trust accounts — through foreign exchange businesses registered under Article 8 of the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act. Capital transactions, which under Article 3 of the Act include deposits, lending, securities and overseas real estate, require advance reporting under FETA Article 18; certain methods of payment or receipt require reporting under Article 16; and some payments to foreign countries may require permission under Article 15. Depending on the transaction the report is made to a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor, and holding and transfer remain subject to sanctions, AML/KYC, tax and reporting requirements. This does not guarantee that any resident may open any particular account.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate non-resident accounts through foreign exchange businesses registered under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act — external accounts and non-resident foreign currency trust accounts for foreign-currency funds, and non-resident Korean-won accounts and non-resident free-transfer Korean-won accounts for won funds (Foreign Exchange Transactions Regulations Article 2-6-2). Certain transactions require transaction-specific reporting to a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor (for example FETA Article 18 capital transactions), and repatriation is not unconditional; account opening remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, tax and each institution's requirements. There is no entitlement to any particular account or service.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Cross-border business payments and receipts run through foreign exchange businesses registered under Article 8 of the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act. Certain methods of payment or receipt require advance reporting under FETA Article 16 — settlement by offsetting a claim, settlement outside the period set by the Minister, payment to or from a person who is not a party to the transaction, and payment or receipt made without going through a foreign exchange agency — and capital transactions require reporting under Article 18, alongside sanctions, AML and reporting rules. This does not establish an unrestricted choice of invoice currency, which the Act does not govern and which depends on the contract and applicable rules.
rules.exchange_controls: South Korea regulates foreign exchange through the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, administered by MOEF and the Bank of Korea. The Act sets procedures in three areas — transaction type, payment and receipt, and method of payment and receipt. Current-account payments and receipts are substantially liberalised, while capital transactions involving large fund movements are subject to transaction-specific notification or permission through foreign exchange banks, the Bank of Korea Governor, or MOEF. The Korean won is not fully internationalised. This is a regulated framework — not an absence of exchange controls and not full liberalisation of the capital account.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Currency conversion and cross-border payments in South Korea are provided through foreign exchange banks and other institutions authorised under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act within the Bank of Korea / MOEF framework. These authorised intermediaries apply the Act's notification, permission and reporting procedures according to transaction type; authorisation does not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price.

countries.country_overview: The United Arab Emirates applies a convertible dirham pegged to the US dollar alongside a supervisory framework centred on the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) for licensed banking and regulated exchange-business activity. Customs and traveller transparency measures complement that framework rather than imposing retail exchange quotas: traveller declarations focus on bearer instruments, cash, jewellery, and precious metals above published thresholds rather than banning foreign currency outright. Interpreted together, the Emirates present as a predominantly open-account environment with AML/CFT and customs reporting obligations layered on cross-border carriage and financial-institution workflows.

summary.traveler: Visitors and residents may move foreign currency broadly freely, subject to traveller declaration rules when declared items exceed AED 60,000 in combined value across cash, bearer instruments, jewellery, and precious metals, using approved customs procedures (including designated digital declaration channels where applicable).
summary.business: Business invoicing and bank transfers are unconstrained by classic exchange-control ceilings in the sovereign sense used elsewhere; AML/CFT and licensing rules still govern intermediaries trading currency and moving funds at scale.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Inbound travellers may carry foreign currency without a legislated statutory cap analogous to rigid import licences. When the traveller carries currencies, cheque-like bearer forms, jewellery, or precious metals whose combined declarable valuation exceeds AED 60,000, UAE customs doctrine expects a declaration aligned with traveller-transparency publications and ICP-aligned digital facilitation at covered ports. Household members under eighteen are not ordinarily required to lodge a standalone declaration beyond inclusion on a guardian declaration where facts support that treatment. Omitting mandated declarations where threshold facts exist is prosecuted as customs evasion risk rather than a routine paperwork preference.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Departure differs operationally from arrival even when headline policy remains permissive: travellers leaving still face the AED 60,000 combined declarable corridor for cash-like and jewellery categories, but the supervisory emphasis shifts to outbound reporting and AML monitoring on later bank or wire corridors. Capital repatriation of salaries, divestment receipts, or investment proceeds is ordinarily not withheld by denomination-specific quotas; compliance teams instead scrutinise sourcing and screening on higher-value corridors. Institutional channels therefore remain the pragmatic choice for sizeable movements that would otherwise collide with traveller-only declaration mechanics.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: Federal traveller declaration standards align on a combined AED 60,000 reporting trigger across cash, negotiable instruments without a named payee, jewellery, and precious metals for passengers aged eighteen and above. The measure is grounded in anti-money-laundering transparency rather than a permit to carry only up to that mark. Officials provide structured declaration forms plus, on selected crossings, interoperable electronic submission consistent with ICA/ICP public guidance. Accuracy matters because valuation disputes feed enforcement channels separate from benign tourist exchanges below reporting facts.
rules.resident_holding_rules: UAE residents maintain AED and multicurrency deposits domestically subject to universal banking AML standards rather than nationality-based holding prescriptions. Everyday conversion between dirhams and majors occurs through authorised institutions where CBUAE licence classes govern who may run exchange counters versus full banking. Residents remitting abroad use SWIFT-like rails with institution-level checks; there is no parallel household foreign-currency ceiling published like hard exchange-control jurisdictions. Relationship managers still expect documentation on unusually large legacy cash deposits.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-resident individuals and corporates open AED or foreign-currency accounts with documentation typical of international banking centres. Repatriation of operating profits, sale proceeds, or payroll savings is not administratively throttled by sovereign conversion permits in the classic sense, though banks apply sanctions screening and correspondent-bank constraints. Non-residents engaging in mainland commercial activity coordinate with licensing authorities separately from FX mechanics. Digital wallets and PSP partnerships expand retail access but inherit the same compliance obligations.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: UAE entities invoice cross-border counterparties in foreign currency without coercion to forcibly surrender proceeds into AED at a punitive spread. Settlement may therefore remain offshore or route through correspondent nostros as commercial contracts dictate. Any firm selling exchange as a standalone product must hold Central Bank approvals under prevailing exchange-business regulation tiers rather than operating as an unregulated bureau. Consolidated groups still centralise treasury under policies that AML teams audit irrespective of denomination choice.
rules.exchange_controls: Administrative parlance distinguishes true exchange controls—mandatory approvals per transaction—from the Emirates' supervisory posture, which concentrates on peg maintenance through monetary instruments and regulated institutions while keeping current-account style flows largely liberal. Profit repatriation, services exports, and re-invoicing frameworks do not require pre-clearance dossiers analogous to guarded-capital regimes. Where tension appears, it is typically compliance-driven delays at bank level rather than sovereign denial of lawful conversion.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Liquidity for tourists and corporates flows through multinational banks, local champions, licensed exchange houses, and airport concessions with published boards. Payments rails include instant domestic transfers where supported and cross-border wires with correspondent cut-offs. Corporates leaning on treasury workstations integrate FX hedging externally while domestic spot needs are satisfied OTC. Operational friction concentrates on onboarding due diligence—not on statutory quotas—when aligning with FATF-aligned programmes.

countries.country_overview: The United Kingdom operates a fully liberalised foreign-exchange regime with no general exchange controls since 1979. The framework is governed by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). There are no restrictions on current or capital account transactions for residents or non-residents.

summary.traveler: Travelers may bring in or take out unlimited amounts of foreign currency and British Pounds. No declaration is required for amounts below £10,000 (Great Britain) or €10,000 (Northern Ireland, when travelling to or from non-EU countries outside the UK).
summary.business: Businesses and individuals enjoy full freedom to hold, transfer, convert and repatriate foreign currency through authorised banks and financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency and sterling may be freely imported. Declaration to Border Force is required when carrying cash of £10,000 or more into Great Britain, or €10,000 or more into Northern Ireland from a non-EU country outside the UK, or the equivalent in foreign currency. An advance declaration may be submitted online up to 72 hours before travel; declaration on arrival is also permitted.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Residents and non-residents may freely export foreign currency and sterling. Declaration to Border Force is required when taking out cash of £10,000 or more from Great Britain, or €10,000 or more from Northern Ireland to a non-EU country outside the UK, or the equivalent in foreign currency. Non-residents may repatriate the full amount of currency declared on entry.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales): cash of £10,000 or more, or its equivalent in foreign currency, must be declared to Border Force when entering or leaving the UK. Northern Ireland: cash of €10,000 or more, or its equivalent, must be declared when travelling between Northern Ireland and a non-EU country outside the UK. These thresholds apply to cash and specified monetary instruments including notes and coins, bearer bonds, and signed travellers' cheques; for Northern Ireland the obligation also covers money orders, gold coins, bullion, and prepaid cards. Declarations are administered by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) through Border Force and derive from UK anti-money laundering legislation.
rules.resident_holding_rules: UK residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in foreign currency or GBP. Cross-border payments and repatriation of funds are handled freely through authorised financial institutions.
rules.exchange_controls: The United Kingdom maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised for both current and capital account transactions.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks, licensed money exchange houses, and ATMs throughout the UK.

countries.country_overview: The United States Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) is the central bank and sets monetary policy, while U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) administer cross-border currency reporting. The United States has a free-floating exchange-rate arrangement — the exchange rate of the US dollar is determined freely in the foreign-exchange market — and, under IMF Article VIII, maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, with no multiple currency practices, except for restrictions maintained solely for security reasons. Capital-account movements are separately regulated. The US dollar is the world's primary reserve currency.

summary.traveler: Travelers may carry unlimited US dollars or foreign currency, but any person transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate — cash or monetary instruments — into or out of the United States must file a Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) with CBP at the border. Amounts of USD 10,000 or less require no declaration.
summary.business: For current international transactions, businesses and individuals can make and receive payments and transfers without exchange restrictions under the United States' IMF Article VIII status, except for measures maintained solely for security reasons. Foreign-currency account access, repatriation, and capital-account movements are governed separately and remain an open evidence gap pending the US OECD reservation schedule.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency and US dollars may be imported without limit or prohibition. Any person bringing more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) into the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with a CBP officer at the port of entry.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: US dollars and foreign currency may be physically transported out without a maximum amount, but transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate currency or covered monetary instruments requires FinCEN Form 105.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The reporting threshold is USD 10,000. Under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340, transporting an aggregate amount exceeding that figure across the US border triggers a mandatory Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) to CBP. This traveler border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveler declaration.
rules.resident_holding_rules: The United States does not maintain a general exchange-control regime over residents' foreign-currency holdings: under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, the US reservation schedule contains no general capital-movement reservation restricting residents' holding, conversion, transfer, or repatriation of foreign currency. Its reservations are limited to enumerated sectoral inward direct investment and a small-issues securities-registration carve-out for non-resident issuers. Account access remains subject to sanctions, AML/KYC, tax, information-reporting, and prudential requirements.
rules.non_resident_rules: For non-residents, the US schedule under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements contains no general reservation restricting ordinary transfer or repatriation; the recorded reservations concern enumerated inward-investment sectors and limited securities-registration treatment for non-resident issuers. This does not entitle every non-resident to every bank account or service: onboarding remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, information-reporting and withholding, and each institution's requirements.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: For current international transactions, payments and transfers are not subject to general exchange restrictions under the United States' IMF Article VIII status, except for measures maintained for security reasons. This finding does not establish rules on invoice denomination or capital-account transactions.
rules.exchange_controls: The United States has a free-floating exchange-rate arrangement and, having accepted IMF Article VIII, maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, with no multiple currency practices — except for restrictions maintained solely for the preservation of national or international security, notified to the IMF. This finding covers current international transactions; capital-account movements are governed separately under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements and the US reservation schedule.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Ordinary currency conversion and cross-border payments operate through regulated US financial institutions and money-services businesses, subject to BSA/AML, sanctions, tax, reporting, and institution-specific controls. Currency dealers or exchangers and money transmitters are money services businesses that must register with FinCEN under the Bank Secrecy Act and maintain applicable compliance programs.

rules.resident_holding_rules.section: OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, Annex B, United States reservation schedule (page 134). The US lodges reservations only on List A, I/A direct investment in enumerated strategic sectors and List A, IV/B1-B2 (small-issues securities-registration for non-resident issuers); no general capital-movement reservation restricts residents' holding, conversion, transfer, or repatriation. Institutional secondary evidence.

rules.non_resident_rules.section: OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, Annex B, United States reservation schedule (page 134). The recorded reservations concern enumerated inward-investment sectors and small-issues securities-registration for non-resident issuers; no general reservation restricts ordinary non-resident transfer or repatriation. Institutional secondary evidence.

rules.banking_conversion_practicality.section: FinCEN — Money Services Business (MSB) Registration. Establishes that currency dealers/exchangers and money transmitters are money services businesses that must register with FinCEN (Treasury) and comply with Bank Secrecy Act obligations — the claim-specific source for the regulated-institution routing of ordinary currency conversion and cross-border payments. Not sourced from the OECD absence of reservations.
